t: Minimum Adjacent Swaps to Partition Array
o: Classify each element: class 0 if x < a, class 1 if a ≤ x ≤ b, class 2 if x > b. A 'good' array is exactly one whose class sequence is sorted (all 0s, then 1s, then 2s). The minimum number of adjacent swaps to rearrange a sequence into a sorted-by-key order equals the number of inversions of the keys — pairs i < j with class[i] > class[j] — because each adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly ±1, and equal-class elements are interchangeable so their internal order never matters. Example 1: classes [0,1,0,1,2,2] have one inversion (the 1 before a 0) → 1 swap. Example 2: classes [2,1,1,0] have 3+3+... let's count: pairs (2,1),(2,1),(2,0),(1,1)no,(1,0),(1,0) = 5 → matches. Example 3: classes [0,1,1,2] are sorted → 0.
k: Map the problem to sorting a ternary key sequence; the answer is its inversion count.
Each adjacent swap changes the inversion count by exactly 1, so the inversion count is a tight lower bound and achievable.
Since there are only 3 classes, inversions can be counted in O(n) with running counters — no BIT/merge sort needed.

a.i: Directly compute the class of each element and double-loop over all pairs, adding 1 whenever an earlier element has a strictly larger class than a later one. This is the definition made literal and is instantly verifiable against the examples.
s: For every pair i < j with class[i] > class[j], add 1 to the answer.

a.i: Scan left to right keeping how many elements of each class have been seen. When we meet an element of class c, every previously seen element of a class greater than c must eventually be swapped past it — that contributes cnt[c+1] + ... + cnt[2] swaps. Summing these contributions over the scan counts every inversion exactly once, in linear time.
s: Keep counters cnt[0..2] initialized to zero and ans = 0.
For each element compute its class c.
Add cnt[2] (+ cnt[1] if c == 0) to ans, then increment cnt[c].
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) work per element

w: Always present the reduction to inversions first — it is the crux. Use the O(n) counter sweep for the final solution (merge sort / BIT would also work but is overkill for 3 keys). Pitfalls: boundary classification (x == a belongs to the middle, x == b too), forgetting the modulo, and assuming elements must be sorted by value rather than merely grouped. Follow-ups: reconstruct an optimal swap sequence, generalize to k groups, or handle a circular arrangement.
